name: Ptolemy the son of Abubus
charge: Murdering Simon the high priest and two of his sons at a banquet in his own castle
summary: Ptolemeus the son of Abubus was made captain in the plain of Jericho and had abundance of silver and gold, for he was the high priest’s son in law; his heart was lifted up, he thought to get the country to himself, and he consulted deceitfully against Simon and his sons to destroy them (1 Maccabees 16:11-13). When Simon came down to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas, Ptolemeus received them deceitfully into a little hold called Docus which he had built, made them a great banquet, and hid men there; and when they had drunk largely he and his men rose up, took their weapons, came upon Simon in the banqueting place, and slew him and his two sons and certain of his servants (1 Maccabees 16:14-16).
offenseFull: The teaching gives this case a name from the street, the back door, and defines it exactly: being taken down by somebody close to you, a family member or a friend, because that is the one direction you are not watching. The reason it names for it is the same one the record gives, which is that the man has watched you get something and cannot stand it: his heart being lifted up, he thought to get the country to himself (1 Maccabees 16:13). He had the position, the money and the marriage, and he had all three from the man he killed.

The setting was ordinary and the victim was at work. Simon was visiting the cities that were in the country and taking care for the good ordering of them, and came down himself to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas, in the hundred threescore and seventeenth year, in the eleventh month, called Sabat (1 Maccabees 16:14). Ptolemeus received them deceitfully into a little hold called Docus which he had built, made them a great banquet, and hid men there; and when Simon and his sons had drunk largely, he and his men rose up and took their weapons and came upon Simon in the banqueting place and slew him and his two sons and certain of his servants (1 Maccabees 16:15-16). The writer says plainly what was done: in doing this he committed a great treachery and recompensed evil for good (1 Maccabees 16:17). The law curses the man that smites his neighbour secretly and the man that takes a reward to slay an innocent person (Deuteronomy 27:24-25), and the wisdom says that whoever rewards evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house (Proverbs 17:13); and the psalm had already described the shape of it, a familiar friend, trusted, who ate bread with him (Psalms 41:9).

The teaching sets the wise man’s rule against the whole scene, that an enemy is never to be trusted, that though he humble himself and go crouching a man should take good heed and beware of him, that he is not to be set beside you nor allowed to sit at your right hand, because when he has overthrown you he will stand up in your place and seek your seat; that he will speak sweetly with his lips while in his heart he imagines how to throw you into a pit, and that he will weep with his eyes but if he finds opportunity he will not be satisfied with blood (Ecclesiasticus 12:10-16). The banquet hall was built for it, and the men were already in the room.
judgmentFull: The book records no sentence executed on him. It records the rest of the plot failing. He wrote to the king to send him a host to aid him, promising to deliver him the country and the cities; he sent others to Gazara to kill John, and letters to the captains to come to him for silver and gold and rewards, and others to take Jerusalem and the mountain of the temple (1 Maccabees 16:18-20). But one ran before to Gazara and told John that his father and his brethren were slain, and that Ptolemeus had sent to slay him also (1 Maccabees 16:21). Hearing it, John was sore astonished, and he laid hands on the men that had come to destroy him and slew them, for he knew that they sought to make him away (1 Maccabees 16:22).

So the country the man had reached for was not his, and the son he had sent men to kill took his father’s place and his father’s work, and the acts of John and his wars are written in the chronicles of his priesthood from the day he was made high priest after his father (1 Maccabees 16:23-24). The teaching uses the case as a warning about who is allowed near the seat: the treachery was possible only because Ptolemeus had been given rank, wealth and a place in the family, and the record leaves his own end unwritten while it keeps writing about the house he tried to destroy.

text.text: Moreover in the plain of Jericho was Ptolemeus the son of Abubus made captain, and he had abundance of silver and gold:
For he was the high priest’s son in law.
Wherefore his heart being lifted up, he thought to get the country to himself, and thereupon consulted deceitfully against Simon and his sons to destroy them.

Now Simon was visiting the cities that were in the country, and taking care for the good ordering of them; at which time he came down himself to Jericho with his sons, Mattathias and Judas, in the hundred threescore and seventeenth year, in the eleventh month, called Sabat:
Where the son of Abubus receiving them deceitfully into a little hold, called Docus, which he had built, made them a great banquet: howbeit he had hid men there.

So when Simon and his sons had drunk largely, Ptolemee and his men rose up, and took their weapons, and came upon Simon into the banqueting place, and slew him, and his two sons, and certain of his servants.
In which doing he committed a great treachery, and recompensed evil for good.
Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly. And all the people shall say, Amen.
Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. And all the people shall say, Amen.
Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house.
Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
Never trust thine enemy: for like as iron rusteth, so is his wickedness.

Though he humble himself, and go crouching, yet take good heed and beware of him, and thou shalt be unto him as if thou hadst wiped a lookingglass, and thou shalt know that his rust hath not been altogether wiped away.

Set him not by thee, lest, when he hath overthrown thee, he stand up in thy place; neither let him sit at thy right hand, lest he seek to take thy seat, and thou at the last remember my words, and be pricked therewith.
Who will pity a charmer that is bitten with a serpent, or any such as come nigh wild beasts?
So one that goeth to a sinner, and is defiled with him in his sins, who will pity?
For a while he will abide with thee, but if thou begin to fall, he will not tarry.
An enemy speaketh sweetly with his lips, but in his heart he imagineth how to throw thee into a pit: he will weep with his eyes, but if he find opportunity, he will not be satisfied with blood.
Then Ptolemee wrote these things, and sent to the king, that he should send him an host to aid him, and he would deliver him the country and cities.
He sent others also to Gazera to kill John: and unto the tribunes he sent letters to come unto him, that he might give them silver, and gold, and rewards.
And others he sent to take Jerusalem, and the mountain of the temple.
Now one had run afore to Gazera and told John that his father and brethren were slain, and, quoth he, Ptolemee hath sent to slay thee also.
Hereof when he heard, he was sore astonished: so he laid hands on them that were come to destroy him, and slew them; for he knew that they sought to make him away.
As concerning the rest of the acts of John, and his wars, and worthy deeds which he did, and the building of the walls which he made, and his doings,
Behold, these are written in the chronicles of his priesthood, from the time he was made high priest after his father.
